name: Questioning Your Own Sources
title: Questioning Your Own Sources
answer: Questioning your own sources is the practice of checking the origin, methods, funding, and current status of every work you cite before treating it as evidence. In literature review and evidence synthesis this means asking whether a paper has been retracted, corrected, or contradicted, and whether its claims survive contact with the full text. The practice applies to both manual reviews and AI-assisted workflows, where extracted claims can drift from their source. This page sits within The AI Researcher's literature review and evidence synthesis collection, which holds 135 research papers and 10,555 claims extracted from research works as a working library.

sections.body: Questioning your own sources is the practice of checking the origin, methods, funding, and current status of every work you cite before treating it as evidence. In literature review and evidence synthesis this means asking whether a paper has been retracted, corrected, or contradicted, and whether its claims survive contact with the full text. The practice applies to both manual reviews and AI-assisted workflows, where extracted claims can drift from their source. This page sits within The AI Researcher's literature review and evidence synthesis collection, which holds 135 research papers and 10,555 claims extracted from research works as a working library.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on direct access to primary sources: publisher pages, preprint servers, institutional repositories, and registries of retractions and corrections. Bibliographic databases and reference managers supply metadata, while AI extraction pipelines can pull claims, but every extracted claim must be checked against the original paper. This site links to the original paper rather than to secondary summarization tools, so that readers can verify the source themselves. Supporting catalogues here include 91 AI books, 801 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 674 glossary terms for cross-checking terminology and methods.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method begins with a structured appraisal of each source: authorship, funding, conflicts of interest, peer review status, sample size, data availability, and code sharing. Reviewers then compare any extracted claim against the full text, checking for selective reporting, p-hacking, or citation of retracted work. For AI-assisted synthesis, the same checks apply to machine-extracted claims, which can be incomplete or misattributed. A source is questioned again when new evidence appears, such as a correction, retraction, or failed replication.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on provenance and integrity. A source may be under copyright or a restrictive licence, and reusing figures or long excerpts without permission creates legal risk. The greater risk is epistemic: relying on a retracted, fraudulent, or non-replicated paper can propagate false findings into a synthesis. Conflicts of interest, missing ethical approval, and patient consent problems also bear on whether a source should carry weight. Provenance records typically note the version of record, any corrections, and the date the source was last checked.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward automated source verification, with tools that flag retracted papers, detect image duplication, and compare claims against registered protocols. Persistent identifiers and versioned evidence syntheses are making it easier to track when a source changes after publication. Open data and code badges, along with preprint and replication databases, are expanding the set of signals a reviewer can check. Over time, questioning your own sources may become a continuous, machine-assisted audit rather than a one-time step.
